questions.question: Continued fraction expansion of `7/22`?
options: [0; 3, 7], since 7/22 = 0 + 1/(3 + 1/7) decomposes cleanly via Euclid
[0; 3, 6], since 7/22 ≈ 0.318 reduces via floor-and-flip sequence to this list
[7; 22], a single layer of the integer parts before any inversion happens
[0; 22, 7], reading the divisor sequence directly from naive long division

questions.question: What is a convergent of a continued fraction?
options: A best rational approximation pₙ/qₙ obtained from truncating after n terms
A geometric series formed by multiplying successive partial quotients together
A continued radical that arises after rationalizing each denominator step
The decimal expansion of the original real number truncated to n digits
questions.explanation: Convergent pₙ/qₙ from truncating [a₀; a₁, …, aₙ]. Best rational approximation: no p'/q' with q' ≤ qₙ is closer to x.

questions.question: Legendre's theorem on continued fractions states: if `|x − p/q| < 1/(2q²)`, then:
options: p/q is a convergent of the continued fraction expansion of x — exact match
p/q approximates x within machine epsilon for q-bit floating-point arithmetic
p/q must be a Stern-Brocot mediant of two consecutive convergents of x
p/q gives a Bezout coefficient pair via the Euclidean algorithm on (p, q)
questions.explanation: Legendre: any rational p/q within 1/(2q²) of x is a convergent of x's CF. Core of Wiener's attack.

questions.question: Wiener's attack on RSA recovers `d` when:
options: d < n^(1/4)/3 — small private exponent appears as a convergent of e/n
d > n^(1/2) — large private exponent reveals d via Pollard-rho on (e, d)
d shares small gcd with φ(n) — Bezout coefficients leak d through Euler
d ≡ 1 (mod p) — d's residue equals one allowing direct CRT factoring
questions.explanation: Wiener (1990): if d < n^(1/4)/3, then k/d is a convergent of e/n (where ed = kφ(n) + 1). Walk convergents of e/n, test each, recover d.

questions.question: Why does using a small private exponent `d` (e.g. d = 3) appeal to implementers, but break RSA?
options: Small d speeds decryption ×log(n)/log(d); but d < n^(1/4) makes Wiener trivial
Small d enables CRT decryption with two passes only, halving the work cleanly
Small d prevents timing attacks since the exponent is too short to leak any bits
Small d compresses certificate size in TLS handshake messages by 256 bytes each
questions.explanation: Decryption cost is O(log d). Picking small d would 100× speed it up, but Wiener breaks it. Modern keygen picks d ≈ n; small e (65537) is fine since encryption is rarely the bottleneck.

questions.question: How does CFRAC (Continued Fraction Factorization) factor n?
options: Use convergents of √n to find x² ≡ smooth (mod n), then linear-algebra for squares
Use convergents of e/n to recover d, then derive p, q from φ(n) = ed − 1
Use convergents of 1/n to detect periodicity in the decimal expansion of 1/n
Use convergents of (n − 1)/n to recover Carmichael λ(n) and split via Euler
questions.explanation: CFRAC (Morrison-Brillhart 1975): x² ≡ y (mod n) from convergents of √n give small |y|, more likely smooth. Predecessor of QS; L_n[1/2, √2] complexity.

questions.question: What is the period of the continued fraction expansion of `√d` for non-square d?
options: Always periodic; period bounded by O(√d · log d) — Lagrange's theorem on quadratic irrationals
Always finite; the algorithm terminates after O(log d) iterations for any d
Always infinite and non-periodic; √d has no exploitable structure as a CF
Periodic only when d ≡ 1 (mod 4); otherwise infinite and aperiodic in nature
questions.explanation: Lagrange: real x has eventually periodic CF iff x is a quadratic irrational. √d for non-square d: purely periodic after a₀ = ⌊√d⌋.

questions.question: Boneh-Durfee improved Wiener's bound to which value via Coppersmith lattice methods?
options: d < n^0.292 — modest gain over Wiener's n^0.25, uses small-roots lattice attack
d < n^0.5 — square-root bound, matching the BSGS / Pollard-rho generic limit
d < n^0.75 — leaves Wiener-style attacks behind by exploiting partial-key leakage
d < n — any d is recoverable in polynomial time given sufficient ciphertext samples
questions.explanation: Boneh-Durfee (1999): d < n^0.292 via Coppersmith's small-roots / lattice. Conjectured tight bound is d < n^(1/2). Practical lesson: pick d ≈ n.
